quiz.q: What does `expr?` do when `expr` evaluates to an `Err(e)`?
options: It panics immediately
It returns `Err(e)` (converted if needed) from the enclosing function right away
It silently ignores the error and continues
It logs the error and continues with a default value
quiz.explain: `?` on an Err returns early from the enclosing function with that error (running it through From::from first). On Ok, it unwraps the value and execution continues.

quiz.q: Why does `?` only work inside a function that returns `Result` or `Option`?
options: It's an arbitrary syntax restriction with no deeper reason
Because `?`'s early return has to return a Result/Option from the enclosing function, and there's nowhere for that to go otherwise
Because Result and Option are the only types with a Debug impl
It actually works in any function, this is a common misconception
quiz.explain: `?` desugars to an early `return Err(...)` (or `return None`). If the function's return type isn't Result/Option, that return has nowhere valid to go, so the compiler rejects it.

quiz.q: What is `expr?` roughly equivalent to, written out as a match?
options: `match expr { Ok(v) => v, Err(e) => return Err(e.into()) }`
`match expr { Ok(v) => return v, Err(e) => v }`
`expr.unwrap()`
`match expr { Ok(v) => Some(v), Err(e) => None }`
quiz.explain: `?` unpacks Ok(v) into v and continues, or returns Err(e) (converted via From) from the function immediately on Err — exactly what that match spells out.

quiz.q: What extra step does `?` perform on the error value that a plain `return Err(e)` would not?
options: It logs the error to stderr automatically
It calls `From::from` on the error, converting it into the function's declared error type if needed
It clones the error
It wraps the error in an Option
quiz.explain: `?` calls From::from on the error so a function can return one error type while `?`-ing through several different underlying error types, as long as a From conversion exists.

quiz.q: A function returns `Result<i32, ParseIntError>`, but you use `?` on something that fails with `std::io::Error`, with no `From<io::Error> for ParseIntError` impl. What happens?
options: It compiles fine; the io::Error is silently discarded
It compiles and converts using Debug formatting
It's a compile error — there's no way to convert the error into the declared error type
It panics at runtime instead of failing to compile
quiz.explain: `?` needs a From conversion path to the function's declared error type. Without one, the compiler rejects the code with a type mismatch on the `?`.

quiz.q: What does `fn main() -> Result<(), E>` let you do?
options: Nothing new — main can never return a value
Use `?` directly inside main, since main itself now returns a Result
Skip writing Ok(()) at the end of main
Automatically catch all panics in the program
quiz.explain: Since `?` needs a Result/Option-returning enclosing function, giving main a Result<(), E> return type lets you use `?` at the top level too.

quiz.q: In `fn main() -> Result<(), std::num::ParseIntError> { let n: i32 = "123".parse()?; Ok(()) }`, what does `Ok(())` mean?
options: Success, with no meaningful value — () is Rust's empty type
An error containing an empty string
The function is still running
A placeholder that must later be replaced with a real value
quiz.explain: `()` (unit) is Rust's 'nothing of interest' type. Ok(()) means the function succeeded but has no value to hand back besides that success.

quiz.q: Does `?` work on `Option<T>`, not just `Result<T, E>`?
options: No, `?` is exclusive to Result
Yes — inside a function returning Option, `?` unwraps Some or returns None immediately
Only in unstable/nightly Rust
Only if the Option contains a Result
quiz.explain: `?` works the same way on Option: it returns the inner value on Some, or returns None immediately from the enclosing (Option-returning) function.

quiz.q: Besides changing the error path, what must you still write explicitly on a function's success path when using `?`?
options: Nothing, `?` handles both paths
An explicit Ok(value) (or Some(value)) at the end — `?` only rewrites the error/early-return side
A call to .unwrap()
A separate match statement
quiz.explain: `?` only handles the early-return-on-failure side. The function's normal return still needs to explicitly wrap the successful value in Ok(...) or Some(...).

flashcards.front: What does `expr?` do on Ok(v) vs Err(e)?
flashcards.back: On Ok(v): unwraps to v and execution continues. On Err(e): immediately returns Err(e) (converted via From if needed) from the enclosing function.

flashcards.front: Why must the enclosing function return Result or Option to use `?`?
flashcards.back: `?`'s early-return path returns an Err/None from the enclosing function. If that function's return type isn't Result/Option, there's nowhere valid for the early return to go, so it's a compile error.

flashcards.front: What does `?` do to the error value that a plain early return wouldn't?
flashcards.back: It calls From::from on the error, converting it into whatever error type the function declares — so `?` can auto-convert between different underlying error types.

flashcards.front: What happens if `?` needs to convert error type A into error type B but no From<A> for B exists?
flashcards.back: Compile error — the `?` has no way to perform the conversion. Fix by widening the return type (e.g. to Box<dyn Error>) or writing the From impl yourself.

flashcards.front: What does `fn main() -> Result<(), E>` enable?
flashcards.back: It lets you use `?` directly inside main, since `?` requires the enclosing function to return Result/Option, and now main does.

flashcards.front: Does `?` still require an explicit Ok(...)/Some(...) on the success path?
flashcards.back: Yes. `?` only handles the failure/early-return side. The function's normal (non-early) return still needs to wrap the value: `Ok(value)` or `Some(value)`.

flashcards.front: Does `?` work on Option<T> as well as Result<T, E>?
flashcards.back: Yes — inside a function returning Option<T>, `?` unwraps Some(v) to v, or returns None immediately on None.
